title: OLTP vs OLAP & Warehouses
subtitle: Watch one revenue report choke a checkout database, then see how a warehouse and a pipeline fix it.
learn: How OLTP workloads (many tiny reads and writes) differ from OLAP workloads (few huge scans)
Why row storage suits transactions and column storage suits analytics
How ETL and ELT move data from the live database into a warehouse or lake
Why running analytics on the production database hurts customers
When to pick a warehouse, a data lake, or both

steps.title: Why does checkout slow down at 9am?
steps.body: A shop keeps 500 million orders in one Postgres-style database. Checkout is fast: p99 latency (the time that 99 percent of requests beat) is about 8 ms. Every morning an analyst opens a dashboard titled revenue by day, and suddenly shoppers see slow or timing-out checkouts. Same database, same data. What changed? The kind of question being asked, not the amount of traffic.
steps.idea: Two workloads can be harmless alone and destructive together on the same database.
steps.caption: Healthy checkout, one analyst about to ask a big question.

steps.title: Transactions: many tiny operations
steps.body: OLTP (online transaction processing) means thousands of small operations per second, each touching one or a few rows: insert this order, read this user's cart, update this stock count. Each must be fast and correct. Databases built for this store each row's fields together on disk, so one row is one cheap read or write, usually found through an index. In the animation a shopper inserts an order and gets 'committed' back in about 8 ms.
steps.idea: OLTP is point reads and writes by key, optimized for latency and correctness.
steps.caption: Shoppers write and read single rows in milliseconds.

steps.title: Analytics hits the live database
steps.body: Now the analyst runs SELECT day, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY day. It must read every one of the 500 million rows. At roughly 200 bytes per row that is about 100 GB. Even at an optimistic 2 GB/s that is around 50 seconds of heavy disk and CPU use. It can also push the pages checkout keeps in memory out of the buffer cache (the RAM that holds recently used disk pages). Checkout queries now wait behind it, and p99 jumps from 8 ms to 900 ms.
steps.idea: A full-table scan competes for the same disk, cache and CPU that transactions need.
steps.caption: The big scan starves checkout of cache and I/O.

steps.title: Row store vs column store
steps.body: A row store keeps all fields of one order side by side, which is perfect for fetching a whole order. A column store keeps all values of one column together, so the revenue query reads only the date and amount columns: about 16 bytes per row instead of 200, or 8 GB instead of 100 GB. Similar values sit together too, so they compress very well, often 3 to 10 times. That shrinks 8 GB to roughly 1 to 3 GB (2 GB here). This is an illustration of what the same report would cost on a column layout.
steps.idea: Columns let analytics read only what it needs, and compress better; rows make single-record access cheap.
steps.caption: The same data laid out by column: far fewer bytes to scan.

steps.title: Copy data out: ETL
steps.body: We cannot just move everything to a column store, because checkout still needs fast row writes. So we keep both and copy. In classic ETL (extract, transform, load) a pipeline pulls changes from the OLTP database, cleans and reshapes them on its own workers, then loads finished tables into the warehouse. Reading changes from the database log (change data capture) puts far less load on the database than rescanning tables.
steps.idea: The OLTP database stays the source of truth; analytics works on a copy.
steps.caption: The pipeline extracts changes and loads the warehouse.

steps.title: Dump first, transform later: ELT
steps.body: Modern warehouses scale compute elastically, so many teams flip the order: ELT (extract, load, transform). Raw data lands first, either straight in the warehouse or in a data lake, which is cheap object storage holding files such as Parquet or JSON in any shape. Transformations then run as SQL inside the warehouse. The lake also feeds machine learning and data nobody has modeled yet. Table formats like Iceberg or Delta on top of lake files let one copy be queried like a warehouse (a lakehouse).
steps.idea: A lake stores raw data cheaply and flexibly; a warehouse stores modeled data for fast SQL.
steps.caption: Raw files land in the lake, then the warehouse transforms them.

steps.title: The same report, off the hot path
steps.body: OLAP (online analytical processing) means few queries that each scan huge amounts of data and aggregate it. The analyst now runs the revenue report on the warehouse. It reads two compressed columns (2 GB), spread across many nodes in parallel, and answers in about a second. Checkout never notices, and p99 stays at 8 ms, because the OLTP database is not queried for the report (only the light change feed still reads from it).
steps.idea: OLAP is built for big scans and aggregates; isolating it protects transactions.
steps.caption: The warehouse answers the report; checkout is untouched.

steps.title: The price: freshness and complexity
steps.body: The copy is never instant. With change capture the warehouse may lag by seconds to minutes; with a nightly batch job, up to a day. You also now run a pipeline that can break, duplicate rows, or drift from the source. Warehouses are poor at single-row updates, so do not point your app at one. Pick the lag the business actually needs. A read replica shields checkout but is still a row store, so the report stays slow (see the Replication lesson).
steps.idea: You trade data freshness and operational effort for isolation and fast analytics.
steps.caption: The warehouse is a slightly stale copy fed by a pipeline.

steps.title: Two workloads, two systems
steps.body: OLTP serves many small, correct, low-latency row operations, so it uses row storage and indexes. OLAP serves few huge scans and aggregates, so it uses column storage and parallel scans. Do not run the second on the first. Move data with ETL or ELT, keep raw history in a lake if you want flexibility, and serve reports from a warehouse. Start with a warehouse; add a lake when you have raw, unstructured or ML data.
steps.idea: Match the storage layout and system to the access pattern, and keep analytics off the transaction path.
steps.caption: Transactions on the left, analytics on the right.

quiz.q: A report needs SUM(amount) over 500 million rows of a 40-column table. Why is a column store usually much faster than a row store here?
options: It stores fewer rows overall
It reads only the amount column, and that column compresses well
It skips the need for aggregation
It keeps all data in memory by default
quiz.why: A column store reads just the columns the query needs, and similar values in one column compress strongly, so far fewer bytes come off disk.

quiz.q: Why can one heavy analytics query make checkout slow even though it only reads data?
options: Reads always lock every table for writing
Read queries are replicated to shoppers
It increases the number of rows in the table
It competes for disk, CPU and buffer cache with transactions
quiz.why: The scan saturates I/O and CPU and can push hot pages out of cache, so small transactional queries wait. Reads do not need to block writes for this to hurt.

quiz.q: A warehouse is fed by a nightly batch job. What is the main cost?
options: Checkout gets slower while the job runs on the OLTP database
Reports can be up to a day stale and the pipeline is another system to run
The warehouse can no longer use column storage
Analysts must query the OLTP database directly
quiz.why: A copy is never instant: a nightly batch means reports lag by up to a day, and the pipeline itself can break or drift. That freshness and operational effort is the price of isolation.

quiz.q: A team lands raw JSON and CSV exports in cheap object storage first and models them into tables later, only when someone needs them. Which approach is this?
options: A data lake, often feeding ELT
ETL into an OLTP database
Row-based sharding
A write-through cache
quiz.why: Storing raw files first and transforming afterwards is the data lake plus ELT pattern; classic ETL transforms before loading.

quiz.q: Your app needs to update one customer's address and show it back instantly. Where should that live?
options: Only in the warehouse, since it holds all data
In the data lake as a new file each time
In the OLTP database, with the warehouse updated later by the pipeline
In the dashboard tool
quiz.why: Warehouses are tuned for big scans, not frequent single-row updates. The OLTP database is the source of truth and the warehouse catches up afterwards.

cheatsheet.def: Online transaction processing: many small, fast reads and writes of individual rows, such as orders and carts. Needs low latency and strong correctness.
Online analytical processing: few queries that scan and aggregate huge volumes of history, such as revenue by region. Needs throughput, not single-row speed.
Row stores keep a record's fields together (good for point access). Column stores keep each column together (good for scans, compression).
ETL transforms data before loading it into the target. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse using SQL.
A column-oriented analytical database holding cleaned, modeled data, queried with SQL by analysts and dashboards.
Cheap object storage of raw data in open file formats (for example Parquet). Flexible, but needs structure added before it is easy to query.
Reading a database's change log to stream inserts, updates and deletes downstream, with less load than repeated full table queries.
Never point heavy analytics at the production OLTP database. Use a copy, with a freshness lag the business can accept.
